note: How to do an old technique in a modern kitchen. MAKE TODAY is not a new recipe, it is the same ancestral dish, cooked tonight. The ingredients stay traditional (that is the whole point: ghee, not vanaspati; gur, not refined sugar, see displacements.json), and only the *method* is translated: equipment that no longer exists, technology that makes it convenient, and a healthy substitute where something is genuinely unavailable. A shortcut that costs the dish its character is noted rather than taken. Matching is by `matches` against a recipe's method steps. These are equipment equivalences, not historical claims, anyone with a kitchen can check them, which is why they carry no source field.

techniques.archaic: roasting directly on charcoal or embers
techniques.modern: roast directly on a gas flame, turning every 2-3 minutes until the skin blackens and the flesh collapses, about 10-12 minutes. No gas: grill under an oven broiler on the highest setting, turning once.
techniques.keep: the direct flame. The smoke is the dish, not a side effect. An oven bake without any flame contact gives a different food.
techniques.convenience: a gas hob does this unattended in a way a charcoal fire never did

techniques.archaic: grinding on a stone (sil-batta, quern), pounding in a mortar
techniques.modern: a mixer grinder in short pulses, scraping down between them. Add liquid a spoon at a time rather than all at once.
techniques.keep: a coarse texture. A stone crushed and tore; a blade cuts, and running it continuously makes a smooth paste the original never was. Pulse, do not blend.
techniques.convenience: minutes instead of the better part of an hour

techniques.archaic: fermenting by ambient warmth, overnight or longer
techniques.modern: an oven with only the light on, or an instant pot on its yogurt setting, holds roughly 30-35°C. In a cold house, a warm cupboard works.
techniques.keep: the time. Warmth speeds fermentation but does not replace it, a batter rushed at high heat sours without rising properly.
techniques.convenience: removes the seasonal problem: the same batter that rose in a Deccan summer will not rise in a Delhi January without help

techniques.archaic: cooking in an earthen or clay pot
techniques.modern: a heavy-bottomed pan, or a cast-iron or clay handi if you have one. Lower the flame slightly against a thin modern base.
techniques.keep: slow, even heat. Earthenware held heat gently and let a little moisture through; a thin steel pan scorches where a clay pot simmered.

techniques.archaic: steaming over water, in cloth or a covered vessel
techniques.modern: any steamer, an idli stand, or a colander over a covered pan of simmering water.
techniques.keep: the lid, and a full boil underneath. This one has barely changed in a thousand years.
techniques.convenience: an electric steamer or pressure cooker with the weight off does it without watching

techniques.archaic: fumigating with asafoetida smoke, agarwood or fragrant resin
techniques.modern: the dhungar method: sit a small steel bowl in the finished dish, put a lit piece of charcoal in it, drip a little ghee on, cover immediately for 2-3 minutes.
techniques.keep: the covered pause. The smoke has to be trapped or it does nothing.
techniques.convenience: no substitute for this one. Liquid smoke is a different flavour and says so.

techniques.modern: an oven at its highest setting with a preheated baking steel or heavy tray, or a cast-iron tawa on a high flame for breads.
techniques.keep: fierce heat, and a hot surface to slap the dough onto. A moderate oven bakes; a tandoor sears.

techniques.archaic: wrapping in leaves before roasting or steaming
techniques.modern: banana leaf where it is sold, it is worth seeking out, because the leaf flavours the food. Otherwise baking parchment, then foil.
techniques.keep: the leaf if you can get it. Foil holds steam but adds nothing; the original was a wrapper and a seasoning at once.

techniques.archaic: deep-frying in a wide vessel of oil or ghee
techniques.modern: a kadai or deep pan, oil at 175-180°C, a pinch of dough should rise within a couple of seconds without browning at once.
techniques.keep: the fat the record names. Frying in the traditional fat is the dish; swapping in a refined seed oil is the substitution this project exists to point at.
techniques.convenience: an air fryer will not reproduce this. Shallow-frying in less oil changes texture but keeps the fat honest, which is the better trade.

techniques.archaic: stretching dough thin with a pesini or by hand
techniques.modern: a rolling pin on a lightly floured board; rest the dough 20-30 minutes first so it stretches instead of springing back.
